title: Organic Chemistry I for Life Sciences
description: Structure, stereochemistry, substitution, elimination, and carbonyl chemistry taught through mechanism and reactivity rather than reaction memorization.

modifications: Clarified the typical E2 answer option as anti-periplanar; atypical syn elimination is not presented as equally typical.

Expanded the week-1 resonance and acid-base prototype with formal-charge and arrow auditing, conjugate-base stability comparisons, a hypothetical pKa equilibrium example, and solvent and mechanism limits.

Expanded the week-5 SN1/SN2 prototype with a conditional mechanism comparison, rate-law consequences, synthetic concentration changes, geometric stereochemistry, and ion-pair limits; linked registered primary OpenStax sections.

Expanded the week-7 elimination prototype with E1/E2/E1cB step order, rate-law models, beta-hydrogen inventory, anti-periplanar and trans-diaxial constraints, and qualified alkene-regioselectivity reasoning.

Expanded the week-9 carbonyl prototype with carbonyl polarization, charge-audited tetrahedral intermediates, addition-versus-acyl-substitution criteria, leaving-group/resonance comparisons, and biomolecular context.
MIT OCW 5.12 Organic Chemistry I, Spring 2005 calendar was checked for aromaticity/EAS placement and used as a curriculum comparator only; the new lesson is original.

Added original aromaticity and electrophilic aromatic-substitution instruction with cyclic electron counting, sigma-complex reasoning and directing effects; combined four related primer/expanded pairs in the proposed schedule. The 11-block grouped sequence remains unmeasured and makes no semester-equivalence claim.

Added an original reaction-energetics reading with formative practice in the existing week 2. MIT OCW 5.12 Spring 2005 calendar and UCI OpenCourseWare Chem 51A lecture list are link-only scope comparators recorded in a new scope crosswalk; no source text, figure or problem is imported.

outcomes.description: Draw valid resonance contributors and predict nucleophile/electrophile roles.
Use substrate, nucleophile, solvent, and leaving group to distinguish mechanisms.
Relate functional-group reactivity to biomolecular synthesis and degradation.

lesson_objectives.description: Rank acidity using conjugate-base stabilization.
Use resonance without moving atoms or violating valence.
Predict how substrate structure and solvent affect substitution.
Connect mechanism to stereochemical outcome and rate law.
Distinguish E1 and E2 pathways.
Predict alkene products while stating regioselectivity assumptions.
Explain why carbonyl carbon is electrophilic.
Predict addition versus substitution from the carbonyl derivative.
Rank acyl derivatives by reactivity toward nucleophilic acyl substitution and relate the ranking to their biological roles.
Calculate the protonated fraction of an ionizable side chain at a given pH and predict its charge and nucleophilicity.
Model the steady-state level of a nonenzymatic modification as a balance of modification and turnover, and explain why long-lived proteins accumulate damage.
Use substrate structure, nucleophile strength, solvent and leaving group to predict whether substitution follows SN1 or SN2, and write each rate law.
Predict the stereochemical outcome at a stereocenter (inversion or racemization) and count possible stereoisomers.
Calculate enantiomeric excess and composition from optical rotation, and explain why stereochemistry matters for biological activity.
Check formula, valence-electron and unsaturation constraints.
Trace valid resonance and electron-pair movements.
Compare acid/base equilibrium with rate-based reactivity.
Normalize conformer populations with stated degeneracy.
Assign and transform the supplied Fischer configuration.
Distinguish descriptors, optical sign and symmetry-reduced counts.
Track selected substitution/elimination pairs and stereoelectronic conditions.
Calculate competing-route rates, branching and conversion.
Qualify mechanism inference under fixed-environment assumptions.
Track carbonyl addition/collapse and donor charge/proton changes.
Calculate stipulated adduct and hydrolysis balances.
Evaluate activation and product evidence in the preserved case.
Identify alpha positions and resonance-compatible enolate flow.
Map aldol atom connectivity and addition/dehydration inventories.
Evaluate stereochemical and crossed-selectivity limits.
Combine formula and constructed spectral constraints.
Calculate integrals/splitting within their model domain.
Distinguish identity, amount, purity and stereochemical evidence.
Calculate conversion and competing product amounts.
Distinguish branching, recovery and calibrated stereochemical amounts.
Evaluate product claims with independent structural/material evidence.
Summarize raw peak reports and determine supplied baseline/gain calibration.
Calculate calibrated pair amounts, signed excess and amount ratios.
Distinguish reporting response, optical identity, absolute configuration and purity evidence.
Classify a cyclic π system as aromatic, antiaromatic or nonaromatic from its conjugation, geometry and electron count.
Explain the addition–elimination sequence of electrophilic aromatic substitution and show where the ring temporarily loses aromaticity.
Predict the broad directing pattern of a substituent on a monosubstituted benzene and state when the product distribution cannot be inferred from directing labels alone.

Explain the addition–elimination mechanism of nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) and predict how the position of an electron-withdrawing group and the identity of the leaving group affect an aryl halide's reactivity.
Predict usual hydrohalogenation and hydration regiochemistry for an unsymmetrical alkene and state the mechanistic assumption.
Distinguish carbocation, halonium-ion and hydroboration pathways by their stereochemical outcomes and rearrangement limits.
Check alkene addition products with atom, stoichiometric-equivalent and unsaturation bookkeeping.
Predict carbonyl products of standard terminal-alkyne hydration routes and explain enol-to-carbonyl tautomerization.
Distinguish partial alkyne reduction to cis or trans alkene from complete reduction to an alkane.
Check alkyne reaction products with formula, degree-of-unsaturation and hydrogen-equivalent balances.
Track the donor alpha carbon and acceptor carbonyl through a stipulated crossed-aldol addition.
Balance formulas for a one-donor/one-acceptor addition and a later water loss.
Use a formula-based unsaturation count and reconcile it with rings and multiple bonds.
Compare synthetic qualitative observations and integrated proton counts without inferring calibrated amount.
Identify stereogenic elements without assigning configurations that the evidence does not determine.
Track a constrained aryne formation and nucleophile atom map.
Close atom, hydrogen and unsaturation ledgers through aryne addition.
Distinguish conditional mechanistic branching from original-inventory product fraction.
Evaluate mechanism evidence without overgeneralizing a restricted formation rule.
Audit reaction order by forward compatibility rather than reagent names alone.
Calculate a multistep isolated-yield ledger with explicit definitions.
Verify target formulas and stereogenic substituent identity through a route.
Compare route metrics without treating step count as proof of quality.
Combine original atom placement with a closed product-amount ledger.
Use graph distance and original labels to distinguish mechanistic predictions.
Derive the target formula and distinguish a nonstereogenic addition product.
Close a compatibility-constrained yield report without claiming an observed synthesis.

Relate a standard free-energy difference to an equilibrium constant and to populations for conformer, acid–base and reaction equilibria, separate enthalpy and entropy contributions, and estimate a reaction enthalpy from stipulated bond dissociation energies.
Read a reaction energy diagram to identify transition states, intermediates and the rate-determining step, convert barrier differences into rate ratios, and match the diagram to a rate law.

Apply the Hammond postulate and the distinction between kinetic and thermodynamic control to predict the dominant product under stated conditions, and explain why a catalyst changes rates but not the equilibrium constant.

duration.equivalent_structure: Proposed 12-block scope, not measured workload or a complete university semester. Four compact-primer/expanded-reading pairs remain grouped. Week 2 adds reaction energetics after conformations, the position MIT OCW 5.12 and UCI Chem 51A give it before substitution. A new alkene/alkyne block follows elimination and alkene formation and precedes aromaticity; MIT OCW 5.12 Spring 2005 allocates weeks 5–7 to alkene and alkyne reactions, so this local treatment remains selective. The synthetic-data virtual lab and preserved self-assessment case are practice activities.

lessons.title: Structure, resonance, and acid-base reactivity
lessons.worked_example: A carboxylate has two valid contributors that keep atom positions fixed and distribute charge over both oxygens. For a hypothetical proton transfer from an acid with pKa 5 to a base whose conjugate acid has pKa 9, the same-scale estimate is K≈10^4 toward products; this compares equilibrium preference, not rate.

modules.title: Structure, electron flow and acid–base balance

lessons.title: Structure, electron flow and acid–base balance
lessons.worked_example: Start from C₅H₉NO and independently count 40 valence electrons and two unsaturation units. Do not select a unique structure yet. For a carboxylate contributor exchange, identify the two simultaneous electron-pair movements and verify unchanged atom positions, net charge and carbon valence. For the separate synthetic acid/base pair, subtract the pK_a values in the correct direction to obtain K=10⁴. At imposed pH 6, normalize acid and base ratio 1:10 for the deprotonated fraction 10/11.

modules.title: Conformations, Fischer maps and stereochemical labels

lessons.title: Conformations, Fischer maps and stereochemical labels
lessons.worked_example: Normalize conformer weights 1 and w to get the single higher-state fraction, then replace the higher weight by 2w when two equivalent arrangements are supplied. For the text Fischer map, rank OH,COOH,CH₃,H; determine the clockwise page traversal and reverse because H points toward the viewer. Swapping the horizontal groups reverses the arrangement. Separately count four configurations without symmetry and three in the stipulated meso case. Keep these spatial and statistical examples distinct.

lessons.title: Substitution mechanisms and stereochemistry: predicting SN1 versus SN2 and tracking what happens at a stereocenter
lessons.worked_example: An SN2 rate of 2×10⁻³ × 0.1 × 0.2 = 4.0×10⁻⁵ M/s doubles when the nucleophile doubles; 3 stereocenters allow up to 8 stereoisomers; a rotation of -9.2° against -11.5° means ee = 80%, or 90:10.

lessons.title: Substitution mechanisms: SN1 and SN2
lessons.worked_example: A tertiary alkyl halide in water favors SN1 in the simplified comparison because backside attack is hindered and ionization can form a stabilized carbocation; a chiral secondary substrate reacting by stated concerted cyanide attack undergoes geometric inversion and follows rate = k[RBr][CN-].

lessons.title: Substitution, elimination and competing pathways
lessons.worked_example: Identify the two SN2 pair movements and the three E2 pair movements, checking that leaving and forming bonds match adjacent atoms. For the synthetic parallel network, multiply each second-order constant by its stipulated free reactant concentration to get a=b=0.0020 s⁻¹. Multiply by S₀ for the initial rates, add a+b for substrate decay and normalize a by that sum for the substitution branch. Check product sum against consumed S before interpreting selectivity.

lessons.title: Elimination, alkenes, and stereochemical control
lessons.worked_example: In a cyclohexane chair, E2 requires a trans-diaxial beta hydrogen and leaving group; only an aligned beta hydrogen can form a product. Check both chairs and any population difference before predicting which alkene dominates, because conformation can override a Zaitsev-only prediction.

modules.title: Aromaticity, electrophilic and nucleophilic aromatic substitution

lessons.title: Aromaticity, electrophilic and nucleophilic aromatic substitution
lessons.worked_example: For methoxybenzene, oxygen-lone-pair donation stabilizes the ortho and para sigma-complex contributors, so the broad EAS products are ortho- and para-substituted; directing labels alone do not establish their ratio. Cyclooctatetraene has eight pi electrons, but its nonplanar tub geometry interrupts continuous overlap, so it is nonaromatic rather than antiaromatic under the stated Hückel criteria. These examples show why geometry and mechanism must be checked before using electron-count or directing-effect shortcuts. The ring can also be the electrophile: methoxide adds to C1 of 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene, the Meisenheimer complex places negative charge on C2, C4 and C6 and onto both nitro groups, and loss of chloride restores aromaticity; the 3,5-dinitro isomer, with only meta nitro groups, is far less activated.

modules.title: Carbonyl addition, acyl transfer and proton bookkeeping

lessons.title: Carbonyl addition, acyl transfer and proton bookkeeping
lessons.worked_example: Describe donor-to-carbon and carbonyl-pair-to-oxygen movements for addition, then distinguish collapse with a declared outgoing Z group from an unsupported alkyl expulsion. For the independent adduct model, set D/C=10×0.20=2 and normalize the total 0.10. For the separate time model, calculate remaining 0.100exp(−0.9) and product by subtraction. Finally examine whether a proposed amide mechanism supplies activation, valid proton bookkeeping and product evidence.

lessons.title: Carbonyl chemistry and acyl transfer
lessons.worked_example: A neutral amine adds to an acid chloride carbonyl, forming a tetrahedral intermediate after the C=O pi pair shifts to oxygen. Proton transfers enable collapse; oxygen reforms C=O as chloride leaves, so the net change is acyl substitution rather than simple addition.

modules.title: Enolates, aldol connectivity and atom balance

lessons.title: Enolates, aldol connectivity and atom balance
lessons.worked_example: Identify ethanal's three alpha hydrogens and distinguish its aldehydic hydrogen. Apply the synthetic pK_a difference for reference proton transfer K=100. Label donor C1/C2 and acceptor C3/C4, then connect C2–C3 and retain donor C=O while converting acceptor C=O into the alcohol after proton transfer. Sum formulas for C₄H₈O₂, then subtract H₂O only for the separate dehydration to obtain C₄H₆O. Check the stereocenter and unsaturation count independently.

lessons.title: Functional groups at work in biomolecules: acyl reactivity, ionization and slow chemical damage
lessons.worked_example: At pH 7.4, histidine is 3.8% protonated and lysine 99.92%; with modification at 0.01 per year, a protein with a 10-year half-life reaches a steady-state modified fraction of 0.126, while a 2-day protein reaches 7.9×10⁻⁵.

lessons.title: Spectroscopic constraints and product identity
lessons.worked_example: Compute one unsaturation unit from C₄H₈O₂. Sum synthetic integrals 3+2+3=8 and normalize the first to 3/8. For the selected ethyl ester model, identify three equivalent neighboring methyl protons for the methylene quartet, then two methylene neighbors for the terminal methyl triplet. Check connectivity against the formula and the qualitative carbonyl observation. Finally state which claims remain unresolved: absolute configuration, complete purity and quantitative amount need their own evidence.

lessons.title: Reaction networks, selectivity and evidence
lessons.worked_example: Add effective rates to obtain 0.050 min⁻¹, calculate I at 20 min and subtract from one for conversion. Normalize a by the sum for target branching and multiply that branch by converted amount for P. Recover H from the other branch and check I+P+H=1. Apply recovery only after formation if that additional assumption is supplied. Separately compare the true 7:3 enantiomer amounts with the biased 14:3 peak-channel areas.

modules.title: Virtual lab 1: calibrated peak amounts and enantiomeric excess

lessons.title: Virtual lab 1: calibrated peak amounts and enantiomeric excess
lessons.worked_example: Synthetic blanks identify 3-unit offsets, and two 10 µmol pure standards identify separate reporting gains 2 and 1. Mix_2 calibrated amounts 7 and 3 µmol give signed A excess 40%; blank-corrected areas alone give about 64.7059%. Optical labels do not establish R/S or real sample purity.

lessons.title: Alkene addition: regiochemistry and stereochemistry
lessons.worked_example: For 1-butene, the standard acid-hydration model predicts 2-butanol, while hydroboration–oxidation predicts 1-butanol; HBr addition changes C₄H₈ to C₄H₉Br and lowers DBE from 1 to 0. This stoichiometric and formula check supports the overall product inventory but does not distinguish 1-butanol from 2-butanol or assign a stereoisomer; those conclusions require connectivity and mechanism evidence.

lessons.title: Alkyne hydration and selective reduction
lessons.worked_example: Hydration of propyne is predicted to give acetone by the Markovnikov route or propanal by terminal-alkyne hydroboration after enol tautomerization. One H₂ equivalent reduces an alkyne to an alkene; two give an alkane. These are predicted textbook products, not measured conversion or isolated yield.

lessons.title: Aldol-identity dossier project guide (optional, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: In a separate stipulated acetaldehyde/benzaldehyde paper addition, C2H4O + C7H6O gives C9H10O2 (DBE 5), and loss of H2O gives C9H8O (DBE 6). The beta-hydroxy connectivity O=CH–CH2–CH(OH)–Ph has one stereogenic center; its donor alpha carbon remains CH2.

lessons.title: Benzyne, elimination–addition and atom-map evidence
lessons.worked_example: C6 cannot supply the required hydrogen, so the allowed intermediate edge is C1–C2. Attack at C1 leaves the fixed C4 tag para, distance three; attack at C2 leaves it meta, distance two. Original carbon labels remain fixed even if a product is later renumbered for naming.

modules.title: Multistep synthesis, protection and forward compatibility

lessons.title: Multistep synthesis, protection and forward compatibility
lessons.worked_example: Three distinct operations have 3!=6 orders. The strict constraints require P,N,D, leaving one feasible order. This is a conditional compatibility argument: a real route still needs evidence for selective masking, mask survival and harmless restoration of the aldehyde.

modules.title: Assignment 1: aryl mechanism and atom-map evidence

lessons.title: Assignment 1: aryl mechanism and atom-map evidence
lessons.worked_example: The products are 2×0.75×0.70=1.05 mmol and 2×0.75×0.30=0.45 mmol; 0.50 mmol remains. Their sum is the original 2.00 mmol. The attachment maps must still be established separately: amount arithmetic does not identify which original carbon bears nitrogen.

lessons.title: Assignment 2: protected-route compatibility and evidence
lessons.worked_example: Net methyl addition and protonation add CH4, giving C10H12O2 and DBE five. The alcohol carbon has two identical methyl substituents, so this target does not introduce a tetrahedral stereogenic center there. Formula arithmetic must remain connected to the labeled structure rather than used as identity proof.

modules.title: Reaction energetics: equilibria, barriers and energy diagrams

lessons.title: Reaction energetics: equilibria, barriers and energy diagrams
lessons.worked_example: For a synthetic SN1 profile with TS₁ at 96 kJ/mol, a carbocation at 60 kJ/mol, TS₂ at 68 kJ/mol and products at −20 kJ/mol, K ≈ 3.2 × 10³ at 298 K, ionization is rate-determining so rate = k[RX], the transition-state-theory rate constant is 9.2 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹ with a half-life near 2.1 hours, and a substituent that stabilizes the carbocation by 30 kJ/mol with 70% felt at TS₁ cuts the barrier to 75 kJ/mol and the half-life to about 1.6 s.

grading_policy.attempt_policy: Unlimited formative retries; no summative grade is awarded.
grading_policy.solution_release: Public practice solutions may be shown after an attempt. They are not production exam keys.
grading_policy.late_policy: No deadlines or late penalties exist in this partial package.
grading_policy.appeals: No instructor review workflow is implemented; report ambiguous practice items to repository maintainers.

accessibility.diagram_policy: The seed package contains no imported diagrams; newly authored diagrams require descriptions and individual license tracking.
known_issues: Unicode equations require structured mathematical alternatives and assistive-technology review.

limitations: The four primer/expanded pairs remain grouped in twelve calendar blocks. Twenty-three reading/activity routes now include selected additions, aryne mechanism evidence, multistep compatibility and two new paper assignments. The proposed grouping and workload remain unmeasured and unreviewed; these counts do not establish a complete university semester.
The proposed 12-block content grouping is unmeasured and unreviewed. Graded homework, exams and a full laboratory sequence remain absent; the paper-only project draft is inactive and ungraded.
New parameters and observations are synthetic; selected electron-flow, conformation, ideal-kinetic and reporting models provide no synthesis or handling procedure or biological recommendation.
Public keys and feedback remain formative authoring specifications; practice points are not course grades.
Subject-matter, accessibility and workload review remain outstanding; the original text Fischer diagram has a verbal description but no assistive-technology review.

OpenStax sections are link-only factual references; no teaching text, problem, figure or dataset was imported. MIT OCW 5.12 Spring 2005 is a course-calendar comparator only; no source course asset was adapted.

The optional aldol-identity dossier project is ungraded. Its milestone drafts are private self-checks; no software check evaluates the learner’s written derivation, diagram or interpretation. The proposed schedule and time estimate have not been measured.

New aryne and multistep-synthesis readings fill the previously omitted introductory benzyne/route-planning strands with explicit atom maps and two paper assignments. General synthesis scope, real chemoselective conditions, broad protecting-group chemistry and experimental route validation remain beyond the stated models. Code, prose, structures and reports are not automatically evaluated; workload and qualified review remain open.

Of the 104 numerical answers, 4 require units, 11 check significant figures and 0 check dimensions. Exact structural/stoichiometric counts use integers; new continuous fractions/amounts request three significant figures.

The scope crosswalk compares the comparators' public session and lecture titles with the local readings, not their lectures, problem sets or exams. UCI Chem 51A is the first course of a three-quarter sequence, so it bears only on the first four blocks. Nomenclature and alcohol and phenol reactions remain recorded gaps.
